title: The Public Library: A Changing Institution
context:
The idea of collecting writing in one place is very old, but the earliest libraries were not for the public. The palace library at Nineveh, assembled by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in the seventh century BCE, held tens of thousands of clay tablets, and the famous library at Alexandria sought to gather the knowledge of the known world. Both were royal projects, designed to display power as much as to preserve learning, and access was restricted to scribes and scholars. An ordinary citizen would not have been admitted.

The notion that ordinary people might borrow books developed much later. In the eighteenth century, groups of readers began to form subscription libraries, in which members paid a fee to share a collection. Benjamin Franklin helped to found one in Philadelphia in 1731. Subscription libraries, however, excluded those who could not afford the fee, and the decisive step was to fund libraries from taxation. Britain passed a law in 1850 allowing towns to raise a small local tax for this purpose, and Boston opened a free library for its citizens soon afterwards. Supporters argued that access to books would improve the working classes and, as one reformer put it, draw them away from the public house.

Philanthropy accelerated the movement. Between 1883 and 1929 the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie paid for the construction of over two thousand five hundred libraries around the English-speaking world. He attached a condition: the town had to provide the land and commit public money to the running costs. Carnegie regarded libraries as a ladder for those who wished to educate themselves, since he had used one himself as a boy. Critics, then and now, have questioned whether gifts from a man who had made his fortune in an industry known for harsh working conditions could be welcomed without reservation, and some towns found the maintenance burden heavier than they had expected.

The twentieth century transformed the experience of using a library. Early public libraries kept books in closed stacks, and readers had to ask a clerk to fetch them. The introduction of open shelves, where visitors could browse and choose for themselves, was resisted by many librarians, who feared that books would be stolen. Experience proved otherwise, and borrowing rose sharply. Dedicated children's rooms followed, along with trained staff who could recommend books, and by the middle of the century the library had become a familiar part of town life.

The arrival of the internet led many commentators to predict the death of the library. That has not happened. Visits have fallen in some countries, but remain high in others, and libraries have responded by lending e-books and offering free computers. Many have also taken on tasks that have little to do with books. Staff help unemployed people to write job applications, run language classes for immigrants, and provide a warm, quiet place for those who have nowhere else to go. Not all communities have been able to keep up: in England, hundreds of branches have closed since 2010 as councils have tried to reduce their spending.

This history suggests that the value of a library cannot be calculated simply by counting loans. A library is a form of what sociologists call social infrastructure, a shared space that brings different people together at little cost. Such places are easy to overlook when budgets are discussed, because their benefits are spread widely and appear slowly. Yet once they have gone, they are very difficult to replace.
